title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
text: In this Lab, you will analyze the “hospital_sim” dataset. It contains simulated (i.e., fake) data about 2000 patients with recent visits to 40 hospitals. On level 1, it includes each patient’s customer satisfaction (satisfaction, continuous), time waiting for the doctor (wait_time, continuous), and type of visit (visit_type, discrete: Emergency vs. Routine); and on level 2, it includes each hospital’s identifier (hospital, discrete: H01 to H40), ratio of nurses to patients (nurse_ratio, continuous), and type (hospital_type, discrete: Teaching or Non-Teaching).

title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
Lab 10: Model Comparison
text:
Step 1 (0.5 pts)
Complete Step 1 of our modeling approach by fitting a null model to dat using glmmTMB() (and FML); the outcome variable should be satisfaction and there should be random intercepts per hospital. Calculate the unconditional ICC.

title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
text:
Step 2 (1.0 pts)
Complete Step 2 by adding fixed slopes of the L1 predictors (i.e., wait_time_within and visit_type). Compare the Step 1 and Step 2 models using the LRT. Are these predictors worth including?

title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
text:
Step 3 (1.0 pts)
Complete Step 3 by adding fixed slopes of all the L2 predictors (i.e., wait_time_between, nurse_ratio, and hospital_type). Compare the Step 2 and Step 3 models using LRT. Are these predictors worth including?

title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
text:
Step 4 (1.0 pts)
Complete Step 4 by adding random slopes of both L1 predictors (i.e., wait_time_within and visit_type). Compare the Step 3 and Step 4 models using LRT. Are these random slopes worth including? If not, try them one at a time (instead of both together) to decide if either is worth including on its own.

title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
text:
Step 5 (1.0 pts)
Complete Step 5 by adding a cross-level interaction between hospital_type and visit_type. Compare the Step 4 and Step 5 models using LRT. Is this interaction worth including?

title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
text:
Final LRT Model (0.5 pts)
What is the final model that LRT prefers? Print its parameter table and interpret all of the fixed effects. What does each result tell us about patient satisfaction? (Hint: Assume a strict \(\alpha=.05\) and remember what happens to the interpretation of slopes in a regression with multiple predictors.)

title: Lab 10: Model Comparison
text:
Information Criteria (0.5 pts)
Compare all five models using AIC and BIC. Which model does each metric prefer?

title: Lab 08: Centering and Degrouping
text: Load the necessary packages (tidyverse, lme4, and easystats). You will be using the “popular.csv” dataset, which contains data on 2,000 students nested within 100 classes.

title: Lab 08: Centering and Degrouping
section: Part I: Data Preparation and Baseline Models
text:
Part I: Data Preparation and Baseline Models

Question 1: The “Split, Transform, Join” Workflow
When working with multilevel data, Level 2 variables are repeated for every row in a cluster. If we center or standardize them using the full dataset, the results become biased because larger clusters pull the mean more strongly than smaller ones. To avoid this weighting problem, we use a specific multi-step workflow.

1a. Create a Level 2 dataset with exactly one row per class. In this new dataset, calculate the raw cluster mean of extraversion (call it ext_b) and include the teacher_exp variable. Then, apply grand-mean centering and standardization to both variables to create ext_bc, ext_bs, teacher_exp_c, and teacher_exp_s.
1b. Merge these new Level 2 variables back into the original student-level data. Finally, calculate the within-cluster component of extraversion (ext_wc) by subtracting the cluster mean from the raw score, and create a standardized version (ext_ws). Ensure class is formatted as a factor.



Question 2: The Null Model and ICC
Before adding predictors, we need to establish how much popularity varies between classrooms.

2a. Fit a null (intercept-only) model predicting peer-rated popularity (popular_peers) with a random intercept for class.
2b. Use icc() to find the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). Interpret this value: what percentage of the total variance in popularity is due to differences between classrooms?

title: Lab 08: Centering and Degrouping
text:
Part II: Degrouped Main Effects

Question 3: Fitting Centered Main Effects
By “degrouping” extraversion into within-cluster and between-cluster components, we avoid estimating an “uninterpretable blend” of effects.

3a. Fit a model predicting popular_peers using centered within-cluster extraversion (ext_wc) and centered between-cluster extraversion (ext_bc). Include a random intercept and a random slope for ext_wc by class. Additionally, control for the teacher’s experience level (teacher_exp_c).
3b. Interpret the fixed effect for ext_bc. Does a classroom’s overall level of extraversion significantly predict a student’s popularity after controlling for the student’s own relative extraversion and the teacher’s experience?



Question 4: Standardized Slopes and Interpretation
Standardizing predictors allows us to compare the relative strength of Level 1 and Level 2 effects on the same scale.

4a. Re-fit the model from Question 3, but use the standardized versions of your predictors (ext_ws, ext_bs, and teacher_exp_s).
4b. Interpret the fixed effect for ext_ws. Specifically, how many raw points does popularity change for every 1-SD increase in relative extraversion? Explain in your own words why we leave the outcome (popular_peers) in its raw metric instead of standardizing it globally.

title: Lab 08: Centering and Degrouping
text:
Part III: Interactions and Visualizations

Question 5: Testing Self-Moderation
We can now test if the effect of student extraversion depends on the average extraversion of the class (a compositional interaction).

5a. Fit a model testing the interaction between standardized within-cluster extraversion (ext_ws) and standardized between-cluster extraversion (ext_bs). Retain teacher_exp_s as a covariate and keep the random slope for ext_ws.
5b. Explain why it is absolutely necessary to include the random slope for the Level 1 predictor (ext_ws) when testing this cross-level interaction. What happens to your error rates if you omit it?



Question 6: Probing Contextual Effects
Visuals and slope analysis clarify whether the relationship at Level 1 is consistent across different Level 2 contexts.

6a. Use estimate_relation() to visualize the interaction from Question 5. Plot the relationship between ext_ws and popularity at different levels (quartiles) of ext_bs.
6b. Use estimate_slopes() to probe the interaction from Question 5. Calculate the trend of ext_ws across different quartiles of ext_bs. Based on the results, does the relationship between individual extraversion and popularity remain significant across all classroom contexts?

title: Lab 07: Random Slopes
section: Part I: Random Slopes for Level-1 Predictors
text:
Part I: Random Slopes for Level-1 Predictors
For this section, we will allow the effect of a Level-1 predictor to vary across our clusters.

Question 1: Fitting a Random Slope Model
In previous labs, we assumed the slope for our Level-1 predictor was identical across all clusters. Now, we will let that slope vary across nations by adding a Level-2 deviation.

1a. Fit a model predicting smile with a fixed slope for sex and a random intercept and random slope for sex by nation. Use the generic formula y ~ 1 + x + (1 + x | cluster) using the lmer() function. Assign this model to an object.
1b. Use the model_parameters() function to view your results. Interpret the random slope standard deviation (\(\tau_{11}\)). Specifically, what does this value tell us about the spread of sex differences across nations?



Question 2: Extracting Random Effects
We can extract the specific estimates for each cluster to see how they differ from the overall population average.

2a. Derive the cluster deviations using estimate_grouplevel(fit, type = "random"). Look up the specific (Intercept) and sex deviations for the "USA". Does the USA have a larger or smaller sex difference than the global average? (Hint: Recall that the global fixed effect for males is negative. Think mathematically about how adding a positive deviation changes the absolute magnitude of a negative slope.)
2b. Look at your model output to find the correlation between the random intercept and random slope (\(\tau_{10}\)). What is this value? Drawing on the lecture material, explain why it is generally important to estimate this correlation parameter even if it is not your primary research question.

title: Lab 07: Random Slopes
text:
Part II: Predictions and Shrinkage

Question 3: Best Linear Unbiased Predictions

3a. Extract the Best Linear Unbiased Predictions (BLUPs) using estimate_grouplevel(fit, type = "total"). Look up the specific total predictions for “JPN”. What are the total estimated intercept and total estimated sex slope specifically for Japan?
3b. Explain the concept of shrinkage or partial pooling in your own words. Why is the spread of our sample predictions always smaller than the estimated population spread?



Question 4: Visualizing Effects

4a. Visualize the fixed effects for the average nation using your multilevel model. Extract the relation using estimate_relation() and plot it.
4b. If you were to plot the cluster-specific predictions, the lines for each nation would no longer be parallel. Why does including a random slope cause this visual change compared to a model with only random intercepts?

title: Lab 07: Random Slopes
text:
Part III: Cross-Level Interactions
For this final section, we will test whether a Level-2 predictor can explain the variability we observed in our Level-1 random slopes.

Question 5: Fitting a Cross-Level Interaction

5a. Fit a model testing whether a nation’s wealth (gdp) moderates the effect of sex on smile. Include a fixed interaction between gdp and sex, and be sure to retain the random intercept and random slope by nation. Use the generic formula y ~ 1 + z * x + (1 + x | cluster) as your guide.
5b. Explain why it is absolutely necessary to include the random slope for the Level-1 predictor (sex) when testing this cross-level interaction. What happens to your Type I error rate if you omit it?



Question 6: Interpreting the Interaction

6a. Interpret the fixed interaction effect (\(\gamma_{11}\)). Does the sex difference in smiling significantly differ depending on a nation’s GDP?
6b. Visualize the fixed effects of the cross-level interaction using your multilevel model. Extract the relation using estimate_relation(), specifying both gdp and sex in the by argument, and plot it. How does this visual output support your conclusion from 6a?

title: Lab 06: Random Intercepts
text:
Part I: Null Models
For this section, we will partition the variance in smiling behavior across different nations.

Question 1: Fitting the Empty Model
Empty models, or null models, are models with no predictor variables. They are an excellent first step when learning multilevel modeling (MLM).

1a. Fit a null model predicting smile with a random intercept for nation. You will need to specify the generic formula y ~ 1 + (1 | cluster) using the lmer() function. Assign this model to an object.
1b. Use the model_parameters() function to view your results. In your own words, report and interpret the fixed intercept and the random intercept standard deviation.



Question 2: Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)
We will continue using null models to estimate ICCs.

2a. Calculate the unconditional ICC for your null model. You can extract the variances manually to calculate this, or you can use the convenience functions from the easystats performance package.
2b. Interpret the ICC in the context of this dataset. Specifically, what percentage of the variance in smiling is between nations, and what percentage is within nations?

title: Lab 06: Random Intercepts
text:
Part II: Level-2 Predictors
For this section, we will add a Level-2 predictor to our model. Because a nation’s GDP (gdp_percap_ppp, an indicator of national wealth) is measured at the cluster level, it has no variance within a cluster. Therefore, it has a single, fixed effect across the entire population.

Question 3: Fitting an L2 Predictor
By adding predictor variables to MLMs, we can try to explain or predict variance partitions.

3a. Fit a model predicting smile with a fixed effect for gdp and a random intercept for nation. Use the generic formula y ~ 1 + z + (1 | cluster) as your guide.
3b. Interpret the fixed intercept and the fixed slope of gdp. What does the intercept represent in this context (where the standardized GDP is zero), and what is the expected change in a nation’s average smiling score for a 1 standard deviation increase in GDP? Is this slope statistically significant?



Question 4: The Cost of Ignoring Clustering
It can be tempting to use a simpler model, but ignoring the clustered nature of your data comes with costs.

4a. Fit a standard linear model (OLS) predicting smile from gdp using the lm() function. Then, use compare_parameters(..., select = "se") to compare the standard errors of the OLS model and your MLM from Question 3a. Briefly explain why the standard errors differ and the danger of ignoring clustering.
4b. Visualize the marginal effect of gdp on smile using your multilevel model from Question 3a. Extract the relation using estimate_relation() and plot it.

title: Lab 06: Random Intercepts
text:
Part III: Level-1 Predictors
For this final section, we will test a Level-1 predictor. Level-1 predictors try to explain variance within clusters. We will assume the effect of our L1 predictor is identical across all clusters.

Question 5: Fitting an L1 Predictor

5a. Fit a model predicting smile with a fixed slope for sex and a random intercept for nation. Use the generic formula y ~ 1 + x + (1 | cluster) as your guide. Assign this model to an object.
5b. Interpret the fixed slope of the sex variable. What is the expected difference in smiling scores for this predictor, and is it statistically significant?



Question 6: Visualizing Fixed Slopes

6a. Derive the cluster deviations to see how each nation deviates from the fixed intercept. You can extract these estimates using estimate_grouplevel(fit, type = "random").
6b. Visualize the marginal effect of sex on smile using your MLM by extracting the relation with estimate_relation() and plotting it. Because we only estimated a random intercept and a fixed slope, what assumption does this model make about the effect of sex across different nations?

title: Lab 04: Data Processing for MLM
text:
2 Data Source
Download the following two CSV files from Canvas and save them in your project folder:

anxiety_wide.csv: Contains repeated anxiety scores for 50 patients over 4 weeks.
patient_info.csv: Contains demographic information (Age and Treatment Condition) for those same patients.

title: Lab 04: Data Processing for MLM
text:
3 Instructions

3.1 Setup and Inspection
Create a new Quarto document for your lab report. Load the tidyverse package and read in the two CSV files using read_csv().
Inspect the anxiety_wide object. Note that it is currently in wide format: there is one row per patient, but the anxiety scores are spread across multiple columns (anxiety_wk1, anxiety_wk2, etc.). This format is unsuitable for MLM and must be reshaped.


3.2 Reshape (Pivot)
Create a new object called anxiety_long. Use the pivot_longer() function to transform the wide anxiety data into long format.

Cols: Select the columns that start with the string “anxiety”.
Names: Send the old column names to a new column called "week".
Values: Send the scores to a new column called "anxiety".



3.3 Clean the Data
Look at your new week column. It currently contains character strings (e.g., "anxiety_wk1").
Overwrite the week column using mutate() and parse_number() to convert these strings into clean numbers (e.g., 1).


3.4 Cluster-Level Summaries
We want to determine the minimum (best) anxiety score each patient reached during the study.
Use mutate() to add this as a new column called min_score to your long dataset. You must use the .by argument (or group_by()) to ensure this calculation happens per patient (patient_id).
(Hint: You can use the min() function to find the lowest score).


3.5 Merging Level 2 Data
The file patient_info.csv contains the study condition (Control vs. Treatment) for each person. This is Level 2 data.
Use left_join() to merge this demographic info into your anxiety_long dataset. Join the two tables by the patient_id column.
Verification: View your data to ensure the condition variable now appears for every time point (row) for each patient.


3.6 Visualization
Use ggplot() to create a “spaghetti plot” of the study results:

Map week to the x-axis and anxiety to the y-axis.
Connect the data points with lines (geom_line()).
Group the lines by patient_id so we see individual trajectories.
Color the lines by condition.

Interpretation Question: Based on your plot, does the Treatment group seem to improve (i.e., scores go down) faster than the Control group?

title: Lab 11: Longitudinal Analysis 1
text: In this Lab, you will analyze the “mood_sim” dataset, which contains simulated Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) data from 100 participants collected over a 14-day study period. At Level 1, the dataset includes each participant’s momentary mood score (mood, continuous outcome), whether they had exercised recently (workout, categorical: 0 = No, 1 = Yes), and the hours of sleep they got the night before (sleep, continuous predictor). At Level 2, it includes each participant’s identifier (subject, discrete).

title: Lab 11: Longitudinal Analysis 1
Lab 11: Longitudinal Analysis 1
text:
2. Base Model (1.0 pts)
Fit a multilevel model to dat using glmmTMB(). Predict mood from the fixed effects of the categorical Level 1 predictor (workout), the centered trait continuous predictor (sleep_bc), and the state continuous predictor (sleep_w).
Include random intercepts per subject, as well as random slopes for both Level 1 predictors (workout and sleep_w). Print the model parameters.

title: Lab 11: Longitudinal Analysis 1
text:
3. Cross-Level Interaction & Plotting (1.0 pts)
Expand on your model from Part 2 by adding an interaction between the categorical state predictor and the centered trait predictor (workout * sleep_bc). We are testing whether a person’s average sleep moderates the mood benefits of a daily workout.
Print the parameter summary for this new model. Then, use the easystats package to visualize this interaction.

title: Lab 11: Longitudinal Analysis 1
text:
4. Discrete Autocorrelation (1.0 pts)
Using your model from Part 3, account for the sequence of observations by adding a discrete AR(1) structure to your random effects. Make sure you use the discrete time_d variable you created during data prep.
Computation Warning: Models with autocorrelation structures and random slopes are mathematically complex. It is completely normal for the models from Parts 4 and 5 to take 30 to 60 seconds to run. Please be patient while the optimizer works!
Compare this new Part 4 model to the Part 3 model using a Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT). Did adding the discrete autocorrelation structure improve model fit? (Note: We use an LRT here because the two models are nested).

title: Lab 11: Longitudinal Analysis 1
text:
5. Spatial Exponential Autocorrelation (1.0 pts)
Because participants occasionally missed days, the time intervals in this study are not perfectly equally spaced. Fit a final model that swaps out the discrete AR(1) structure for a Spatial Exponential structure (exp()). Make sure you use the continuous time_c variable you created during data prep.
Compare this Part 5 model to the Part 4 model using AIC and BIC. Which autocorrelation approach provides a better fit for this data? (Note: We must use AIC/BIC here instead of an LRT because the AR1 and Exponential models are not nested).

title: Lab 11: Longitudinal Analysis 1
text:
6. Final Model Interpretation (1.0 pts)
Looking at the parameter tables for your preferred model from Part 5, interpret all of the fixed effects (the intercept, the main effects of workout, state sleep, and trait sleep, and the interaction). What does this model tell us about the factors that influence daily mood?

title: Lab 12: Longitudinal Analysis 2
text:
In this Lab, you will analyze the “focus_sim” dataset. This dataset contains simulated data from 200 employees enrolled in a 6-week productivity training program. We want to understand how their daily focus scores change over the course of the training program and what factors predict those changes.
At Level 1, the dataset includes the specific day of the study the assessment was completed (study_day), the employee’s focus score for that week (focus_score, continuous outcome), and whether they engaged in a mindfulness meditation exercise that week (meditated, dummy coded: 0 = No, 1 = Yes).
At Level 2, it includes each employee’s identifier (subject, discrete) and their baseline motivation for the training program assessed at intake (motivation, continuous predictor).

title: Lab 12: Longitudinal Analysis 2
text:
1. Data Prep (1.0 pts)
Download the “focus_sim.csv” dataset from Canvas, add it to your project folder, and read it into R as a tibble called dat_raw.
Prepare the data for analysis by creating a centered and scaled time variable. The study_day variable records the raw calendar day of the assessment. If we used this raw variable, our intercept would represent focus on Day 0, which is meaningless here. Furthermore, a slope based on raw days would represent daily growth, which might be confusingly small.
Create a new variable called time that centers the days so that 0 represents the first assessment in the study (Day 12) and scales the variable so that 1 unit equals exactly 1 week (7 days).
Also, create a grand-mean centered version of the continuous Level 2 predictor (motivation_c).

title: Lab 12: Longitudinal Analysis 2
text:
2. Unconditional Linear Growth Model (1.0 pts)
Fit an unconditional linear growth model to your prepared dataset using glmmTMB(). Predict focus_score from the fixed effect of your new time variable. Include random intercepts per subject, as well as random slopes for time.
Print the model parameters table using easystats. In 1-2 sentences, interpret the fixed effect intercept and time slope.

title: Lab 12: Longitudinal Analysis 2
text:
3. Unconditional Quadratic Growth Model (1.0 pts)
Now, test whether the trajectory of focus scores is curved. Fit an unconditional quadratic growth model. To avoid multicollinearity problems, use the poly(time, 2) function to generate orthogonal polynomial terms for your fixed and random effects.
Print the model parameters for the fixed effects.

title: Lab 12: Longitudinal Analysis 2
text:
4. Model Comparison (1.0 pts)
Compare your linear model from Part 2 and your quadratic model from Part 3 using the AIC and BIC metrics.
Based on these metrics, which shape best characterizes the growth trajectory of focus scores in this sample?
Once you have identified the best-fitting model, use the estimate_relation() function to plot the predicted growth curve for the average subject across time.

title: Lab 12: Longitudinal Analysis 2
text:
5. Predicting Change: L2 Predictor (1.0 pts)
Moving forward with the best-fitting model from Part 4, let’s try to explain why some employees start with higher focus scores and grow faster than others.
Add the centered time-invariant predictor (motivation_c) to your model. Remember that to test if a Level 2 predictor influences the rate of growth, you must include a cross-level interaction between the predictor and time (motivation_c * time). Keep your random effects the same as in Part 2.
Print the fixed effects. Does baseline motivation significantly predict the starting point of focus scores? Does it significantly predict the rate of linear growth?
Finally, use the estimate_relation() function to visualize this cross-level interaction. Plot the predicted growth curves across time for employees at low, medium, and high baseline motivation (motivation_c=[quartiles]).

title: Lab 12: Longitudinal Analysis 2
text:
6. Predicting Fluctuations: L1 Predictor (1.0 pts)
Finally, we want to explain the observation-specific deviations around each employee’s growth trajectory. Add the time-varying dummy predictor (meditated) to your model from Part 5. Include it as a main fixed effect to test if weeks where an employee meditated correspond to a bump in focus above their expected curve. Also, add it to your random effects bracket to allow the benefit of meditation to vary across subjects.
Print the fixed effects. What does this model tell us about the relationship between weekly meditation and focus scores?

title: Lab 13: Model Evaluation
text: Apply the systematic workflow for multilevel model (MLM) troubleshooting and diagnostics to evaluate, correct, and interpret problematic model outputs.

title: Lab 13: Model Evaluation
text: Apply the systematic workflow for multilevel model (MLM) troubleshooting and diagnostics to evaluate, correct, and interpret problematic model outputs.

title: Lab 13: Model Evaluation
text:
Background
Pretend that you have been hired as a statistical consultant by a large research lab. A junior researcher ran several multilevel models using {glmmTMB} but encountered warnings and confusing diagnostic plots. They have provided you with a document containing their initial model summaries and diagnostic checks. They need your expertise to figure out what went wrong and how to fix it.
Note: These cases represent three independent projects the lab is working on. Treat each case as a separate, unrelated dataset and model.

title: Lab 13: Model Evaluation
text:
Instructions
Review the three independent cases below. Write a professional memo to the researcher addressing the issues. For each case, your memo must include:

Diagnosis: Identify the most likely primary problem based on the specific context clues provided in the case. (You do not need to list every possible cause of a warning, only the one clearly indicated by the symptoms).
Explanation: Explain to the client (in clear, accessible language) why this problem occurs and what it means for their results if left unaddressed.
Solution: Provide explicit instructions on what they need to do to fix the model or verify the robustness of their findings.

title: Lab 13: Model Evaluation
text:
The Cases

Case 1: The Hessian Warning
The client brings you a model where they are predicting a participant’s annual income in raw dollars (ranging from $20,000 to $150,000) using a cognitive reaction time task measured in seconds (ranging from 0.25 to 0.85 seconds). They report that glmmTMB() threw a “non-positive-definite Hessian matrix” warning. They are worried their data is broken.


Case 2: The Pruned Slope
The client was testing their primary lab hypothesis: that a new clinical treatment reduces patient anxiety. Their initial model, which included a random slope for the treatment variable across different clinics, failed to converge (though the variance for the slope was estimated at 0.45). The researcher tells you: “I just removed the random slope for the treatment to get it to run. The new model converged perfectly, and my fixed effect for treatment is significant (\(p < .05\))! We can publish this, right?”


Case 3: The Red Bars
The client ran simulateResiduals() from the DHARMa package to check for outliers. They show you a histogram with a large block of red bars grouped exactly at the 0.0 and 1.0 margins. The researcher is panicking and says: “Traditional Cook’s Distance didn’t show this. DHARMa says I have massive errors, so I think I have to throw away all these participants.”

title: Lab 13: Model Evaluation
text:
Deliverable Format
Submit a 1 to 2 page document formatted as a professional consulting memo (e.g., in formatted text, DOCX, or HTML). You do not need to write new R code. Focus your answers on the statistical concepts, the decision-making workflow, and your theoretical interpretation of the diagnostics.

title: Multilevel Modeling
text:
Course Description
Statistical methods for analyzing multilevel data (e.g., datasets with clustered, nested, or longitudinal structures) using a framework known variously as multilevel, mixed-effects, hierarchical linear, or random-coefficient modeling. The course reviews ordinary least squares regression and then introduces: the challenges posed by multilevel data, tools for processing multilevel data for analyses, and both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian estimation. Core topics include partial pooling, random intercepts, fixed and random slopes, cross-level interactions, model comparison, troubleshooting, applications to repeated-measures and longitudinal data, and thorough diagnostics and reporting. Emphasis is placed on conceptual understanding paired with hands-on analysis in statistical software. Students apply methods to real datasets and complete an independent project.


Learning Outcomes
At the conclusion of this course, students will be able to:

Explain the issues that clustered data cause for the linear model
Contrast the pros and cons of different approaches for clustered data
Prepare a clustered dataset for multilevel analysis in R
Estimate various types of multilevel models in R
Flexibly specify different random effects structures
Interpret the fixed and random effects estimates
Explain the rationale and consequences of partial pooling
Identify the interpretation implied by each centering option
Detail and assess the assumptions made by a multilevel model
Decompose repeated and longitudinal measures into components
Discuss the idea of Bayesian estimation for multilevel models
Discuss the ideas of nested and cross-classified models
